# Antiseptics (strong spirit, chlorinated lime, carbolic acid, iodine) (`antiseptics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by distillation, contagion_theory, chlorine_bleach, hand_hygiene, heat_sterilisation
- Core idea: Antiseptics reduce microbes on living skin. Suitable alcohol-based preparations disinfect intact skin; wine is too dilute, and neither alcohol nor a quick chemical dip sterilises surgical instruments. Clean instruments first, then use a validated sterilisation process. Wash dirt from minor wounds with clean water. Chlorinated lime, phenol and iodine preparations belong to different periods of antisepsis and have different uses and hazards. Lister used carbolic acid in dressings and on equipment; strong phenol can damage tissue, and the smell of chlorine cannot determine a safe dilution.
- Pitfalls:
  - Using wine, beer or ordinary brandy and believing it sterilises
  - Thinking pure spirit is better than diluted; about 70 % works best, and no spirit kills the spores of lockjaw and gangrene
  - Flooding open wounds with strong carbolic or sublimate, which kills tissue and can poison
  - Dipping dirty instruments briefly instead of cleaning them first
  - Spirit near a flame or cautery
- History: egypt: c. 1600 BC – honey and resins on wounds (Edwin Smith papyrus); greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic texts wash wounds with wine and vinegar; europe: 1267 – Theodoric of Lucca uses wine-soaked dressings; 1820s Labarraque's chlorine solutions; 1847 Semmelweis; 1867 Lister's carbolic acid method for compound fractures; 1881 Koch tests disinfectants on bacteria; 1908 Grossich's iodine skin preparation; 1915 Dakin's dilute hypochlorite for war wounds
- Read:
  - Joseph Lister, On the antiseptic principle in the practice of surgery, British Medical Journal (1867)
  - Lindsey Fitzharris, The Butchering Art (2017)
  - Guido Majno, The Healing Hand: Man and Wound in the Ancient World (1975)
